original_text:
–Categories are needed to make sense of all of Earth’s diversity–Scientists have identified close to 2 million different species–Actual estimates of Earth’s diversity are 10-100 million species
–Taxonomyis the discipline of identifying and grouping organisms–Names species–Classifies species into a hierarchy of broader groups
–Systematicsis the study of evolutionary relationships between organisms
explanation: This page introduces methods used to categorize the massive diversity of life on Earth. While scientists have identified approximately 2 million species, estimates of total global diversity range from 10 to 100 million species. Taxonomy is defined as the scientific discipline of identifying, naming, and classifying organisms into a hierarchical system of broader groups. Systematics is the study of the evolutionary relationships that exist between organisms.

questions.q: What is the primary difference between taxonomy and systematics according to this slide?
opts: Taxonomy deals with identifying, naming, and classifying species, while systematics is the study of evolutionary relationships.
Taxonomy focuses on cellular anatomy, while systematics studies global ecosystems.
Taxonomy calculates the total number of species, while systematics names new organisms.
Taxonomy deals with living organisms, while systematics studies extinct species only.
questions.exp: The slide defines taxonomy as the discipline of identifying, grouping, naming, and classifying species, and systematics as the study of evolutionary relationships between organisms.

questions.q: What is the estimated range of Earth's total species diversity compared to the number identified by scientists?
opts: Close to 2 million identified; 10-100 million estimated
questions.exp: The slide states that scientists have identified close to 2 million species, but actual estimates of Earth's diversity are 10-100 million species.
